name: Midwives - we are all at sea but our boats are not the same

content.text: Nurses and midwives are the backbone of healthcare throughout the world. They are the glue that holds together the patient's journey, ensuring that treatment is appropriate and timely. Often nurses and midwives are the first and only point of care in communities, particularly in low resource countries such as Uganda. In recognition of the vital role that nurses and midwives play in providing health services, the World Health Organization (WHO) has designated 2020 as the "Year of the Nurse and Midwife", to celebrate the 200

As skilled professionals, we have devoted our lives to caring for the community throughout the whole life continuum, from pregnancy and childbirth, childhood and adolescence through to adult health, caring for older people and generally meeting everyday essential health needs. We work in every setting including clinics, health centres and hospitals offering screening for a variety of conditions, prevention of disease through education and immunisation, diagnosis and treatment, advice and counselling. We also care not only for the patient but also for their families and loved ones, educating, supporting, comforting and celebrating.
However, we did not expect the COVID-19 pandemic as we celebrated nurses and midwives this year. The pandemic has, to some extent, overshadowed the celebrations but also highlighted the work we do.

I have been working in Uganda for the past three and a half years teaching midwifery and thought you might like a perspective of lockdown here. Uganda has a high maternal mortality rate as well as a very fragile health system. Therefore, a large scale pandemic here would be catastrophic, so when the first case was identified in the middle of March, the response from the government was immediate. All schools and universities were closed overnight, the airport was closed, all non-essential services and shops closed, public transport stopped and there was a ban on using personal cars, even in emergencies. Additionally, there is a 7 pm curfew which is strictly enforced, and you are beaten if you break the curfew for any reason. There are food shortages and there is no financial support for the many who have lost their jobs because of the lockdown.

There are reports that pregnant women in labour have died because they have not been allowed through roadblocks to get to a hospital, and it is difficult to get cancer treatment, surgery services or any routine care amid the lockdown. Uganda has ground to a halt. Nonetheless, women still go into labour and are now forced to give birth in unsanitary conditions without skilled care. Although midwives are still turning up for work, they too have many challenges. One of my students (with a young family herself) is walking two hours each way to work a 12-hour shift looking after nearly 100 women per day in her hospital. Due to the transport restrictions, most of the women walk to the hospital themselves.

Although the lockdown has been effective, just over 100 cases so far, no deaths and half have recovered, the personal and economic repercussions are immeasurable. We will have to see what the maternal death rate is as a result of the lockdown.
Despite the circumstances, this is the best time to train nurses and midwives on how to respond and continue to deliver care.
In response to the emergence of the first case, AKU-SONAM faculty in Uganda developed a two-week online training programme for frontline staff. The course, labeled the

targeted ICU nurses who will be responding to patients who are critically ill after exposure to COVID-19. We interacted with the participants via virtual learning platforms (Moodle and Zoom) and sent them data bundles to ease connectivity. For those who could not access virtual learning platforms, we formed a dedicated WhatsApp group with updates and resources used in the virtual learning sessions. The course was successful and a great learning experience for us, with several other nurses asking for more courses. We are preparing another online course which will focus on infection control and prevention, based on the feedback that was received from the first group, targeting forty participants.
As the rest of the world is fretting over toilet rolls and pasta, we are preparing East Africa to provide the best care in a totally different context.
Happy Year of the Nurse and Midwife!
The writer is a Professor of Midwifery at the Aga Khan School of Nursing and Midwifery. Any opinions expressed are solely those of the writer.
